title: Roman Abramovich: Charity set up to oversee frozen £2.35bn from Chelsea sale
content:
A new charitable foundation aimed at breaking the deadlock between Roman Abramovich and the UK government over the frozen £2.35billion from the sale of Chelsea has formally submitted its application to the UK Charity Commission.

The Foundation for the Victims of Conflict, as it has been named, will be overseen by Mike Penrose, a former UNICEF executive, and includes several other high-profile trustees.

Martin Griffiths, a senior UK diplomat and former United Nations Under-Secretary-General for Humanitarian Affairs and Emergency Relief Coordinator, has been named a trustee, as has Caryl Stern, previously executive director of the Walton Family Foundation.

The Walton Family Foundation, established in the United States by Sam and Helen Walton, the founders of Walmart, is one of the largest philanthropic organisations in America. Stern also served as president and CEO of UNICEF USA, overseeing their fundraising and advocacy initiatives.

Also joining Penrose, Griffiths and Stern as a trustee of the Foundation for the Victims of Conflict is Nimco Ali, a co-founder and CEO of The Five Foundation, a UK-based global partnership dedicated to ending female genital mutilation.

The UK Charity Commission has confirmed to The Athletic that the Foundation for the Victims of Conflict has submitted its application, and it will now be subject to regulatory approval to ensure it meets the legal definition of a charity and that the trustees comply with their legal duties.

A Charity Commission spokesperson said: “We have received an application to register the Foundation for the Victims of Conflict to receive funds from the sale of Chelsea FC and will be assessing this against the legal framework for charitable status to determine if it meets the legal tests to be a charity.

“Our role as regulator is to ensure that organisations entered onto the Register of Charities meet the legal definition of a charity and that trustees comply with their legal duties.”

This application comes at a time when Abramovich and the UK government are still locked in disagreement regarding how the £2.35bn ($3.12bn at current rates) should be spent.

The UK government has long maintained that the proceeds from the Chelsea sale to BlueCo, a consortium led by Todd Boehly and Clearlake Capital, in May 2022 will remain frozen unless Abramovich signs off on it only being spent in Ukraine.

But the new foundation’s intention is for the money to be spent on global causes — as evidenced by the trustees it has appointed — instead of being limited to Ukraine and Ukrainian victims of the Russian war.

This impasse prompted UK Prime Minister Keir Starmer to issue a legal threat to the Russian billionaire in December unless he agrees with their conditions, adding that the “clock is ticking”.

The Athletic has previously reported that Abramovich’s legal team informed the UK government that the proceeds from the Chelsea sale are “wholly” his and that he would fight any attempt to confiscate them.

On April 1, when it emerged that a new foundation was going to be created, a spokesperson for the Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office spelled out that the government will not back down.

“We have been clear from the start that the full proceeds of the sale of Chelsea FC must be used for humanitarian causes in Ukraine,” they told The Athletic. “Our absolute priority remains ensuring the funds reach the most vulnerable in Ukraine who have endured over four years of relentless suffering.”

But in correspondence seen by The Athletic, the Russian oligarch’s lawyers have alleged that the “UK Government appears to be treating this proposed donation as a form of punitive measure against Mr Abramovich”.

Central to this ongoing dispute is the live investigation into Abramovich in Jersey, which included more than $7bn worth of Abramovich-linked assets being seized by the Jersey Royal Court in March 2022.

If the Foundation for the Victims of Conflict receives regulatory approval, there are no guarantees the UK government will release the £2.35bn and further engagement between the two parties is expected in the coming weeks.
